messages.content: How does fasting in Islam compare with the Bahá’í fast?

perplexity.text:
Both are annual daylight fasts centered on spiritual discipline, prayer, and greater awareness of God, but they differ in length, calendar, rules, and exemptions.

| Aspect | Islam | Bahá’í Faith |
|---|---|---|
| **Period** | Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar; normally 29 or 30 days, so its Gregorian dates shift each year.[7] | The Bahá’í month of ʿAlá, normally March 2–20, immediately before Naw-Rúz, the Bahá’í New Year.[1] |
| **Daily fast** | Abstention from food, drink, smoking, and sexual relations from dawn until sunset.[7] | Abstention from food and drink from sunrise until sunset; sexual relations are not prohibited by the fast.[2] |
| **Spiritual purpose** | Worship, God-consciousness, self-restraint, gratitude, repentance, charity, and solidarity with those in need. | Prayer, meditation, spiritual renewal, and detachment from selfish or bodily desires; physical fasting is understood as a symbol of an inward spiritual fast.[1][3] |
| **Who fasts** | Generally healthy, adult Muslims, with exemptions for illness, travel, pregnancy, nursing, menstruation, old age, and other relevant conditions; missed obligatory days may often be made up or compensated according to circumstances. | Generally Bahá’ís aged 15 through 70; exemptions include illness, old age, pregnancy or nursing, travel, and heavy physical labor.[3][6] |
| **Daily rhythm** | A pre-dawn meal (*suḥūr*) and sunset meal (*iftār*) are customary; Ramadan also places strong emphasis on communal worship and charity. | Meals may be taken before sunrise and after sunset, while the period is especially associated with prayer and reflection; the fast is an individual religious obligation rather than one enforced by Bahá’í institutions.[2] |

The closest structural parallel is that both require abstaining during daylight hours and treat fasting as more than simply going without food. The main practical contrast is that Islamic Ramadan lasts roughly a lunar month and includes abstention from sexual activity during daylight, whereas the Bahá’í fast lasts 19 fixed days in early March and does not impose that sexual restriction.[2][7]

current.text:
The two fasts are close in form and differ in length, calendar, scope and the details of the rules. Both are daylight fasts from food and drink, and both are tied to the revelation of a Prophet.

**What they share**
- **Daylight abstention.** The Qur'án says to eat and drink "until the white thread becometh distinct to you from the black thread of the dawn. Then strictly observe the fast till nightfall" ([The Meaning of the Glorious Qur’án (Pickthall)](https://oceanlibrary.com/meaning-of-the-glorious-quran_muhammad/?paraId=para_201&selectionString=the-qur-an_en_8g.0~the-qur-an_en_8g.553)). Bahá'u'lláh says: "Abstain from food and drink from sunrise to sundown" ([The Kitáb-i-Aqdas](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah/?paraId=para_24&selectionString=kitab_i_aqdas_bahai_en-bl3g.0~kitab_i_aqdas_bahai_en-bl3g.390)).
- **Exemptions.** In the Qur'án, the sick and those on a journey fast the same number of other days later, since "Alláh desireth for you ease" ([The Meaning of the Glorious Qur’án (Pickthall)](https://oceanlibrary.com/meaning-of-the-glorious-quran_muhammad/?paraId=para_199&selectionString=the-qur-an_en_8e.0~the-qur-an_en_8e.423)). In the Bahá'í fast, "The traveller, the ailing, those who are with child or giving suck, are not bound by the Fast" ([Directives from the Guardian](https://oceanlibrary.com/directives-from-the-guardian_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_247&selectionString=directives_from_the_guardian_en-bl9m.0~directives_from_the_guardian_en-bl9m.311)). Muslim sources also exempt pregnant women ([A Popular Dictionary of Islam](https://siftersearch.com/library/islam/miscellaneous/ian-richard-netton_a-popular-dictionary-of-islam#p1337)).
- **Link to revelation.** Ramadán is the month "in which was revealed the Qur'án" ([The Meaning of the Glorious Qur’án (Pickthall)](https://oceanlibrary.com/meaning-of-the-glorious-quran_muhammad/?paraId=para_199&selectionString=the-qur-an_en_8e.0~the-qur-an_en_8e.423)). 'Abdu'l-Bahá says the Bahá'í fast follows the same pattern: during such days the Manifestation is occupied with revealing verses and laws, so that "there remains no condition or time for eating and drinking" ([Table Talks of 'Abdu'l-Bahá](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/abdul-baha-corinne_table-talks-of-abdul-baha#p31)). He cites Moses' forty days on Sinai as another example ([Table Talks of 'Abdu'l-Bahá](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/abdul-baha-corinne_table-talks-of-abdul-baha#p31)).

**Where they differ**
- **Length and calendar.** Ramadán is the ninth month of the lunar calendar. It therefore moves through the seasons, starting about eleven days earlier each year ([A Popular Dictionary of Islam](https://siftersearch.com/library/islam/miscellaneous/ian-richard-netton_a-popular-dictionary-of-islam#p1337)) ([Bahai News - Holidays](https://bahai-library.com/newspapers/2000/112500.html)). The Bahá'í fast is nineteen days, the month of 'Alá', and falls from about 2 to 20 March ([Uncompiled Published Letters](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_6112&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl67v.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl67v.537)). It ends with Naw-Rúz as a feast ([The Kitáb-i-Aqdas](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah/?paraId=para_23&selectionString=kitab_i_aqdas_bahai_en-bl3f.0~kitab_i_aqdas_bahai_en-bl3f.958)).
- **Preparation.** The Bahá'í fast is preceded by Ayyám-i-Há, days of "good cheer" and giving to the poor ([The Kitáb-i-Aqdas](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah/?paraId=para_23&selectionString=kitab_i_aqdas_bahai_en-bl3f.0~kitab_i_aqdas_bahai_en-bl3f.958)).
- **Who is bound.** The Bahá'í fast is obligatory from the age of fifteen ([Lights of Guidance](https://oceanoflights.org/lights-of-guidance-baha-i-ocean-en/#:~:text=Regarding%20the%20nineteen%2Dday%20fast,peoples.%22%3Cbr%3E%7Bid%3D%22para2917%22%20ilmid%3D%22bl1rg%22%20type%3D%22par%22%20language%3D%22en%22%7D)). Bahá'u'lláh exempts "those who are weak from illness or age" ([Uncompiled Published Letters](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_6109&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl67s.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl67s.714)). A popular summary gives the age range as 15 to 69 ([Fasting period ends Sunday](https://bahai-library.com/slavin_fasting_period)), though Shoghi Effendi's letter says "until they reach seventy" ([Lights of Guidance](https://oceanoflights.org/lights-of-guidance-baha-i-ocean-en/#:~:text=Regarding%20the%20nineteen%2Dday%20fast,peoples.%22%3Cbr%3E%7Bid%3D%22para2917%22%20ilmid%3D%22bl1rg%22%20type%3D%22par%22%20language%3D%22en%22%7D)).
- **Other restrictions.** The Qur'anic fast also forbids marital relations by day ([The Quran (Rodwell), Sura II. The Cow](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-ii-the-cow_muhammad/?paraId=para_114&selectionString=sura_ii_the_cow_quran_ocean_en-bl8d.0~sura_ii_the_cow_quran_ocean_en-bl8d.494)), and Muslim summaries list this alongside food and drink ([A Popular Dictionary of Islam](https://siftersearch.com/library/islam/miscellaneous/ian-richard-netton_a-popular-dictionary-of-islam#p1337)). The Bahá'í texts I found state the abstention only as food and drink ([Uncompiled Published Letters](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_6112&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl67v.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl67v.537)).
- **Making up missed days.** The Qur'án requires missed days to be made up later ([The Meaning of the Glorious Qur’án (Pickthall)](https://oceanlibrary.com/meaning-of-the-glorious-quran_muhammad/?paraId=para_199&selectionString=the-qur-an_en_8e.0~the-qur-an_en_8e.423)). For a Bahá'í traveller, the Guardian's secretary advised keeping the fast on the days one is not travelling, which is "advisable, but it is not essential" ([Unfolding Destiny](https://oceanlibrary.com/unfolding-destiny_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_3920&selectionString=unfolding_destiny_bahai_ocean_en-bl3ke.0~unfolding_destiny_bahai_ocean_en-bl3ke.247)).
- **Prayer.** The Bahá'í fast is joined to prayer and the daily recitation of the Greatest Name ([Tablets of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá ‘Abbás vol. 1-3](https://oceanlibrary.com/tablets-of-abdul-baha-abbas-vol-1-3/?paraId=para_387&selectionString=tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-blc8.0~tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-blc8.197)). Shoghi Effendi calls it a time of "meditation and prayer, of spiritual recuperation" ([Uncompiled Published Letters](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_6112&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl67v.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl67v.537)). 'Abdu'l-Bahá calls prayer and fasting "the twin pillars that sustain the Law of God" ([Lights of Guidance](https://oceanoflights.org/lights-of-guidance-baha-i-ocean-en/#:~:text=With%20regard%20to%20the,%7Bid%3D%22para5797%22%20ilmid%3D%22bl3pw%22%20type%3D%22par%22%20language%3D%22en%22%7D)).

**The inner meaning**
The Bahá'í texts stress that the outward act is a symbol. Shoghi Effendi writes: "Fasting is symbolic, and a reminder of abstinence from selfish and carnal desires" ([Uncompiled Published Letters](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_6112&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl67v.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl67v.537)). Bahá'u'lláh writes: "Fasting reduceth carnal inclinations, and increaseth spiritual tendencies" ([Tablet on the Fast](https://adibmasumian.com/translations/Bahá’u’lláh-fast-tablet-1/)). 'Abdu'l-Bahá says that "mere abstention from food has no effect on the spirit" ([1911, Ethel S. Stevens - ‘Abbás Effendi, an article in the Fortnightly Review](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/e-s-stevens_1911-ethel-s-stevens-abbas-effendi-an-article-in-the-fortnightly-review#p35)) and that moderation matters ([1911, Ethel S. Stevens - ‘Abbás Effendi, an article in the Fortnightly…](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/e-s-stevens_1911-ethel-s-stevens-abbas-effendi-an-article-in-the-fortnightly-review#p35)). He also says real fasting is "to abstain from carnal desires and the promptings of ego" ([Abdu''l-Bahá in Egypt](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p792)). The Qur'an gives the aim of fasting as that "they may ward off (evil)" ([The Meaning of the Glorious Qur’án (Pickthall)](https://oceanlibrary.com/meaning-of-the-glorious-quran_muhammad/?paraId=para_201&selectionString=the-qur-an_en_8g.0~the-qur-an_en_8g.553)).

**A historical note**
In 'Akká, 'Abdu'l-Bahá and His household kept the Muslim Ramadán. At that time He did not want the believers to keep the Bahá'í fast, and some recalled that He kept both ([Summon Up Remembrance](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/marzieh-gail_summon-up-remembrance-2#p1841)).

I can go on to the Báb's nineteen-day fast in the Bayán, which came between the two.

It brings in 'Abdu'l-Bahá's pilgrim-note explanation of why Manifestations fast, the inner meaning, and a labelled historical note on Ramadán in 'Akká. It needlessly cites a popular summary for the age range.

But it quotes no scripture from either faith. Its citations are bare numbers, and its account of the Islamic purposes is unsourced. It doesn't give the spiritual rationale from the Writings in their own words.

verdict.gaps: B covered the heavy-labour exemption, the Islamic exemption for menstruation, and the meal rhythm (suḥūr and ifṭár), and it said plainly that the Bahá'í fast doesn't restrict marital relations. A lacked these, and it also left out that smoking is included in the abstention.

messages.content: What do Hindu scriptures and the Gospels each teach about what happens after death?

perplexity.text:
Hindu scriptures and the Gospels both teach that death is not the end, but they describe the afterlife very differently.

## Hindu scriptures

- The **ātman**—the true self—is not destroyed when the body dies. The *Bhagavad Gītā* compares the body to worn-out clothing that the self lays aside and replaces.[1][2]
- After death, the self ordinarily continues through **saṃsāra**, the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth. The next embodiment is shaped by **karma**, the moral consequences of one’s actions.[1][2]
- The ultimate goal is **mokṣa**, liberation from saṃsāra. Hindu traditions describe this variously as realization of the self’s relation to Brahman, union with ultimate reality, or eternal nearness to the divine.[2][3]
- Hindu scriptures also describe temporary heavenly or hellish realms, but these are generally not final destinations; when their karmic causes are exhausted, rebirth continues.[4]

## The Gospels

- Jesus’ teaching presents human life as a single earthly life followed by judgment, not an endless cycle of reincarnation. The Gospels speak of the dead being raised and judged by God.[5][6]
- Jesus teaches **resurrection**: the dead will be raised, and people will receive a final destiny. In John, he promises resurrection and eternal life to those who believe in him.[7]
- The final alternatives are described as **eternal life with God** and judgment or punishment for those who reject God’s will. Matthew 25:46 explicitly contrasts “eternal life” with “eternal punishment.”[8]
- The Christian hope is therefore not escape from embodiment but resurrection and renewed life through Christ; Jesus’ own resurrection is presented as the pattern and guarantee of this hope.[6][7]

**In summary:** Hindu scriptures generally teach transmigration through many lives until liberation, while the Gospels teach one earthly life, resurrection, final judgment, and an eternal destiny—life with God or separation from him. These are broad summaries: Hindu traditions differ over the nature of the self and mokṣa, and Christian traditions differ over the details of judgment and hell.

current.text:
**Hindu scriptures teach that the soul outlasts the body and is reborn until it is freed. The Gospels teach one earthly life, followed by resurrection, judgment and eternal life.** The library gave me the Gita and Mahabharata for the Hindu side, and I did not find the Upanishad texts themselves. The Hindu teaching is also not uniform across schools, so the passages below are samples.

The Mahabharata version reads: "as childhood, youth, and decrepitude are in this body, so (also) is the acquisition of another body" ([The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa Vol. 2](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/15475)) ([The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa Vol. 2](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/15475)).
- **What a person holds in mind at death shapes what comes next.** One who meditates on Krishna alone "in putting off his flesh, comes forth to Me." One who "meditated otherwise … goes to what he looked for, … Because the Soul is fashioned to its like" ([The Bhagavad-Gita](https://oceanlibrary.com/bhagavad-gita/?paraId=para_95&selectionString=bhagavad-gita_en_5h.0~bhagavad-gita_en_5h.606)). The Mahabharata gives the same teaching ([The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa Vol. 2](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/15475)). Eliot calls it "the doctrine of the deathbed prayer" ([Hinduism and Buddhism Vol. 2](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/16546)) ([Hinduism and Buddhism Vol. 2](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/16546)).
- **The aim is release, not endless return.** The one who stays even-minded in pleasure and pain "is fit for emancipation" ([The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa Vol. 2](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/15475)).

He also says, "In my Father's house are many mansions… I go to prepare a place for you" ([The Bible (KJV), The Gospel of John](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-gospel-of-john/?paraId=para_529&selectionString=the-gospel-of-john_en_hd.0~the-gospel-of-john_en_hd.90)).

**How the Bahá'í Writings relate the two**
- Bahá'u'lláh teaches that after death the soul "will continue to progress until it attaineth the presence of God" ([Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_474&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_fx.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_fx.1978)). This agrees with both traditions that the soul survives.
- It does not agree with rebirth. Shoghi Effendi's secretary writes that "reincarnation does not exist. We come on to this planet once only," and likens this life to the womb ([Lights of Guidance](https://oceanoflights.org/lights-of-guidance-baha-i-ocean-en/#:~:text=We%20know%20from%20His,%7Bid%3D%22para6890%22%20ilmid%3D%22bl4jx%22%20type%3D%22par%22%20language%3D%22en%22%7D)). Another letter says the Bahá'í view "can in no way be reconciled with certain Indian and Sufi doctrines" of passing from one body to another ([Uncompiled Published Letters](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_5505&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl5nq.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl5nq.497)).
- 'Abdu'l-Bahá describes the Hindu belief that illness is "retribution" for past lives ([The Promulgation of Universal Peace](https://oceanlibrary.com/promulgation-of-universal-peace_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_806&selectionString=promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_p5.0~promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_p5.1396)). Asked about returning, he answers: "In My Father's House are many mansions — many, many worlds! Why would you desire to come back to this particular planet?" ([The Baha'i World: A Biennial International Record, Volume VI (91 and 9…](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/compilations/prepared-under-the_the-bahai-world-a-biennial-international-record-volume-vi-91-and-92-of-the#p7862)). He is using the same Gospel verse quoted above.
- The Writings read the Gospel language symbolically. The resurrection of Christ "could not have been a bodily resurrection" but means "the deliverance of the spirit of Christ and His Cause" ([Uncompiled Published Letters](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_6235&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl6bl.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl6bl.411)). Likewise, whoever receives light from Christ's spirit "finds everlasting life" (['Abdu'l-Bahá's Interpretation of Some Bible Verses (SAQ = Some Answere…](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/compilations/abdul-bahas-interpretation-of-some-bible-verses-saq-some-answered-questions#p137)).

I can look further at how 'Abdu'l-Bahá treats "return" as the return of qualities, using the John the Baptist and Elijah example ([The Promulgation of Universal Peace](https://oceanlibrary.com/promulgation-of-universal-peace_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_806&selectionString=promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_p5.0~promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_p5.1396)).

messages.content: Is Bahá’u’lláh’s detachment the same thing as Buddhist non-attachment?

perplexity.text:
Not exactly. **Bahá’u’lláh’s detachment and Buddhist non-attachment overlap ethically and psychologically, but they rest on different metaphysical foundations.**

- **Common ground:** Both discourage clinging to transient possessions, pleasures, identities, and circumstances. Both aim to free a person from craving, fear, and dependence on impermanent things.[1][5]
- **Bahá’í meaning:** Detachment is primarily **turning the soul toward God**—being free from anything that veils divine love or prevents service. It does not mean rejecting the world or abandoning ordinary responsibilities; Bahá’u’lláh even identifies productive work and self-support as expressions of detachment.[2][6]
- **Buddhist meaning:** Non-attachment generally concerns relinquishing *taṇhā*—craving—and *upādāna*—clinging—through insight into impermanence, suffering, and non-self. Its goal is liberation from the causes of suffering, culminating in nirvana, rather than devotion to a creator God.

So the concepts are **analogous, not identical**. A useful comparison is:

> Bahá’í detachment means “cling to nothing more than God”; Buddhist non-attachment means “cling to nothing,” including a permanent self or metaphysical claim.

This is a simplified contrast: Buddhist traditions differ considerably, and some forms of Buddhism use devotional language. Likewise, Bahá’í detachment is not indifference or emotional coldness; it is meant to support love, moral action, and selfless service.[6][7]

current.text:
They overlap but aren't the same. Both treat clinging to the world as the problem. They differ in what the detachment is for and in how it shows up in a person's life. I'm drawing the Buddhist side only from the two Buddhist texts the library returned, so it is a partial picture.

**What they share**
- A Buddhist discourse traces attachment to desire: "Desire and lust is a cause of attachment" ([Dīghanikāya: Long Discourses](https://oceanlibrary.com/dighanikaya-long-discourses/?paraId=para_1345&selectionString=digha_nikaya_the_long_discourses_of_the_buddha_oce34d6013d3e9976d7693ba158a056b8e3-bl1gr.0~digha_nikaya_the_long_discourses_of_the_buddha_oce34d6013d3e9976d7693ba158a056b8e3-bl1gr.341)). The Buddhacarita says that "when desire is stopped, the attachment to existence is stopped" ([Buddhacarita](https://oceanlibrary.com/buddhacarita_ashvaghosha/?paraId=para_1084&selectionString=life_of_buddha_ocean_buddhism_en_x6.0~life_of_buddha_ocean_buddhism_en_x6.114)).
- Bahá'u'lláh also treats attachment as an obstacle. He tells people to "Disencumber yourselves of all attachment to this world and the vanities thereof," because such attachments prompt people to "walk after your own lusts and covetous desires" ([Surat al-Bayán (The Súrah of the Exposition)](https://hurqalya.ucmerced.edu/node/478/)).
- He also prays to be "detached from my own desires and severed from the attachments of a corrupt inclination" ([Supplications](http://joshuahalltranslations.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/Supplications-by-Bahá’u’lláh.pdf)).

**Where Bahá'u'lláh's detachment differs**

1. **It is detachment toward God.** The Writings speak of being detached "from all else except God" ([Suratu'l-Nus'h (Chapter of Exhortation)](http://www.nayriz.org/template.php?pageName=tablet145&menuStates=000000011010000)). 'Abdu'l-Bahá says the heart should be "attracted toward the Kingdom of God" even while the mind is busy ([Foundations for a Spiritual Education: Research of the Baha'i Writings](https://bahai-library.com/nsa_foundations_spiritual_education)). Detachment is the freeing of the heart for God, and the stilling of desire is not the goal in itself. A Bahá'í compilation says attachment matters because it "distracts the individual from awareness of God" ([Compilation on Detachment](https://bahai-library.com/detachment_bayat)).

2. **It is not withdrawal or asceticism.** Bahá'u'lláh says: "Living in seclusion or practising asceticism is not acceptable in the presence of God... Deprive not yourselves of the bounties which have been created for your sake" ([Bahá’í Sacred Writings](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_781&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bloa.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bloa.711)). A person may enjoy the world's goods "if he alloweth nothing whatever to intervene between him and God" ([Compilation on Detachment](https://bahai-library.com/detachment_bayat)). The standard is moderation ([Compilation on Detachment](https://bahai-library.com/detachment_bayat)).

3. **It is expressed through work and service.** 'Abdu'l-Bahá defines severance as "that man's heart should not be attached to the things of the world." He adds that it does not mean a person should not be occupied with a livelihood, since a useful vocation is "a duty incumbent upon every Bahá'í" ([Abdu'l-Bahá's Visit to California - Notes and Documentation](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/ella-goodall-cooper_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california-notes-and-documentation#p715)). A letter on behalf of Shoghi Effendi, cited by the House of Justice, reports that Bahá'u'lláh called being occupied with a profession and self-supporting "the highest form of detachment in this day" ([Share your time with God](https://bahai-library.com/uhj_share_time_god)).

4. **It includes even-mindedness.** 'Abdu'l-Bahá says that if fortune smiles, one should not be "excessively joyous," and if it leaves, one should not be grieved ([Abdu'l-Bahá's Visit to California - Notes and Documentation](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/ella-goodall-cooper_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california-notes-and-documentation#p715)). This is close to the equanimity people associate with Buddhist practice.

**A point you might not expect:** Bahá'u'lláh pairs detachment with righteousness: "Righteousness and detachment are like unto two most great lights" ([Compilation on Detachment](https://bahai-library.com/detachment_bayat)). So detachment is one of two lights that go together. The other is conduct and service in the world.

A scholarly article in the library says 'Abdu'l-Bahá called the Buddha a major Manifestation of God ([Tablet to Mírzá Abu'l-Faḍl Concerning Questions of Manakji](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_cole_questions_manakji)). On that view the two teachings could share a common root while being expressed differently. The Writings I found don't equate the two concepts.

I can look at how 'Abdu'l-Bahá or Shoghi Effendi speak about the Buddha's teachings in particular if you'd like.

messages.content: Compare the Torah, the Qur’án and the Bahá’í writings on the creation of man.

perplexity.text:
The three traditions agree that humanity is created by one God, originates from earthly matter, and possesses a distinctive spiritual vocation. They differ chiefly in how literally they narrate Adam and Eve, how they understand humanity’s first disobedience, and whether creation is presented as a historical beginning or as a process with deeper symbolic meaning.

## Comparative overview

| Theme | Torah | Qur’án | Bahá’í writings |
|---|---|---|---|
| **First human beings** | Genesis presents Adam as formed from the dust of the ground and animated by God’s breath; Eve is subsequently made as Adam’s companion from his side or rib. Bahá’í commentary explicitly summarizes this Torah account.[1] | Adam is created from clay, dust, or molded earth; humanity’s descendants arise through biological generation. Adam’s mate is created from the same essential nature, and the Qur’án does not name her Eve.[2] | Bahá’u’lláh affirms that all people are created in the God-given nature and that humanity shares one origin and substance. The writings also interpret humanity’s formation as gradual, comparable to the development of an embryo.[3][4] |
| **Image or likeness of God** | Genesis says humanity is created “in the image” and likeness of God. This gives human beings a special status within creation. | The Qur’án emphasizes that God taught Adam the names, honored humanity, and endowed human beings with knowledge, moral responsibility, and vicegerency on earth. | Bahá’u’lláh describes the human reality as a mirror reflecting God’s names and attributes, with the unique capacity to know and love God.[3] |
| **Purpose of human creation** | Genesis portrays humans as responsible for cultivating and governing the earth, while remaining accountable to God. | Humans are created to worship and serve God, act as His trustees on earth, and live morally under divine guidance. | The central purpose is explicitly stated as knowing God and attaining His presence; human potential is realized through free will, spiritual development, and the reflection of divine qualities.[1][3] |
| **Adam and Eve’s disobedience** | Adam and Eve eat from the forbidden tree after the serpent’s temptation. The act introduces shame, alienation, labor, and mortality into the human story. | Both Adam and his mate are involved in the lapse, Satan deceives them, and God accepts their repentance. The Qur’án does not present inherited original sin in the same way as later Christian theology.[2] | The Adam-and-Eve story is generally treated symbolically rather than as a literal account of biological origins. Bahá’í interpretation understands Adam as a Manifestation of God and the fall as conveying spiritual truths about humanity’s relationship to divine guidance.[5] |
| **Human equality** | Genesis gives both sexes a shared human dignity through creation in God’s image, although the two creation narratives describe their origins differently. | Adam and his mate derive from a single soul or common nature, supporting a strong theme of shared human origin and moral equality.[2] | Bahá’í writings make common origin a basis for rejecting human superiority: all were created from the same dust so that no one should exalt himself over another.[4] |
| **Literal or symbolic interpretation** | The Torah presents a narrative account of creation, though Jewish interpretation has long included symbolic and philosophical readings. | The Qur’án presents Adam as a real primordial human and prophet, while its descriptions of human formation use several complementary images—dust, clay, fluid, and stages. | Bahá’í writings do not require a literal reading of Genesis’s creation timetable and reconcile human origins with gradual development and scientific findings.[5] |

## Main similarities

- **Divine initiative:** In each tradition, humanity is not accidental but derives from God’s creative will.
- **Earthly origin:** Dust, clay, earth, or a related material symbolizes human physical dependence and humility.[1][2][4]
- **Distinctive human capacity:** Humans possess a special capacity for knowledge, moral choice, and relationship with God. Bahá’u’lláh describes this as the ability to know and love God and reflect divine attributes.[3]
- **Moral responsibility:** Creation carries an ethical purpose: humans must obey God, care for creation, and develop spiritually.

current.text:
**Short version:** the Torah and the Qur'án both describe a first man made from earth and given life by God. The Bahá'í Writings keep that picture but read it spiritually. They say human beings are made in God's image, and that humanity's physical development was gradual but always human.

**The Torah**
- There are two accounts. In the first, "God created man in His own image, in the image of God created He him; male and female created He them" ([The Tanakh (JPS 1917), Torah - Bereshit (Genesis)](https://oceanlibrary.com/jps-book-of-genesis/?paraId=para_33&selectionString=torah_bereshit_judaism_ocean_en-bl3i.0~torah_bereshit_judaism_ocean_en-bl3i.85)).
- In the second, "the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul" ([The Bible (KJV), Genesis](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-first-book-of-moses/?paraId=para_44&selectionString=the-genesis-prod_en_3x.0~the-genesis-prod_en_3x.109)).
- The Torah then has Adam placed in Eden, Eve made from his rib, the serpent, and the fruit of the tree of good and evil ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_429&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_ex.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_ex.974)).

**The Qur'án**
- Man is made from earth: "We created man of dried clay, of dark loam moulded." ([The Quran (Rodwell), Sura XV. Hedjr](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-xv-hedjr_muhammad/?paraId=para_10&selectionString=sura_xv_quran_ocean_en-bl1i7.0~sura_xv_quran_ocean_en-bl1i7.295)) God then says to the angels, "when I shall have fashioned him and breathed of my spirit into him, then fall ye down and worship him" ([The Quran (Rodwell), Sura XV. Hedjr](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-xv-hedjr_muhammad/?paraId=para_10&selectionString=sura_xv_quran_ocean_en-bl1i7.0~sura_xv_quran_ocean_en-bl1i7.295)).
- The Qur'án also describes how each person is made. It starts "with clay" and goes on to "germs of life", and God then "shaped him, and breathed of His Spirit into him, and gave you hearing and seeing and hearts" ([The Quran (Rodwell), Sura XXXII. Adoration](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-xxxii-adoration_muhammad/?paraId=para_6&selectionString=sura_xxxii_adorations_quran_ocean_en-bl2ut.0~sura_xxxii_adorations_quran_ocean_en-bl2ut.346)) ([The Quran (Rodwell), Sura XXXII. Adoration](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-xxxii-adoration_muhammad/?paraId=para_6&selectionString=sura_xxxii_adorations_quran_ocean_en-bl2ut.0~sura_xxxii_adorations_quran_ocean_en-bl2ut.346)).
- It describes the stages of the embryo: a moist germ, a clot of blood, a piece of flesh, bones clothed with flesh, and then "man of yet another make" ([The Quran (Rodwell), Sura XXIII. The Believers](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-xxiii-the-believers_muhammad/?paraId=para_4&selectionString=sura_xxiii_the_believers_quran_ocean_en-bl26w.0~sura_xxiii_the_believers_quran_ocean_en-bl26w.429)) ([The Quran (Rodwell), Sura XXIII. The Believers](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-xxiii-the-believers_muhammad/?paraId=para_4&selectionString=sura_xxiii_the_believers_quran_ocean_en-bl26w.0~sura_xxiii_the_believers_quran_ocean_en-bl26w.429)).
- The creation is one of dignity: God "moulded thee and shaped thee aright" ([The Quran (Rodwell), Sura LXXXII. The Cleaving](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-lxxxii-the-cleaving_muhammad/?paraId=para_4&selectionString=sura_lxxxii_the_cleaving_quran_ocean_en-bl4t8.0~sura_lxxxii_the_cleaving_quran_ocean_en-bl4t8.222)) ([The Quran (Rodwell), Sura LXXXII. The Cleaving](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-lxxxii-the-cleaving_muhammad/?paraId=para_4&selectionString=sura_lxxxii_the_cleaving_quran_ocean_en-bl4t8.0~sura_lxxxii_the_cleaving_quran_ocean_en-bl4t8.222)).

**The Bahá'í Writings**

1. *Shared motifs.*
   - Bahá'u'lláh keeps the "clay" language but gives it a spiritual sense. "Out of the clay of love I molded thee" ([The Hidden Words of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/hidden-words-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_47&selectionString=the-hidden-words-prod_en_42.0~the-hidden-words-prod_en_42.360)). "Out of the wastes of nothingness, with the clay of My command I made thee to appear" ([The Hidden Words of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/hidden-words-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_311&selectionString=the-hidden-words-prod_en_be.0~the-hidden-words-prod_en_be.732)).
   - He also echoes the "image" of Genesis: "I knew My Love in thee, therefore I created thee; upon thee I laid My Image" ([Abdu'l-Bahá at First Unitarian Church in San Francisco on 6 October](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/core-talks/aminullah-farid_abdul-baha-at-first-unitarian-church-in-san-francisco-on-6-october#p59)).
   - 'Abdu'l-Bahá says: "God has created man after His own image and likeness" ([The Promulgation of Universal Peace](https://oceanlibrary.com/promulgation-of-universal-peace_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_1276&selectionString=promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_127.0~promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_127.911)). For Him this likeness lies in the mind's power to discover "abstract realities" and in the "second birth" into the spiritual world ([The Promulgation of Universal Peace](https://oceanlibrary.com/promulgation-of-universal-peace_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_1276&selectionString=promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_127.0~promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_127.911)).
   - Bahá'u'lláh calls man "the supreme Talisman" and "a mine rich in gems of inestimable value", whose treasures come out only through education ([Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_779&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_od.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_od.1321)).

2. *The Adam story is symbolic.*
   - The House of Justice notes that 'Abdu'l-Bahá, in *Some Answered Questions*, "explains that it cannot be taken literally" ([Lights of Guidance](https://oceanoflights.org/lights-of-guidance-baha-i-ocean-en/#:~:text=Concerning%20the%20story%20of,%7Bid%3D%22para6368%22%20ilmid%3D%22bl45h%22%20type%3D%22par%22%20language%3D%22en%22%7D)).
   - He says that read literally, the account would be "exceedingly strange". He calls it "symbols and divine mysteries" ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_430&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_ey.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_ey.464)) ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_431&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_ez.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_ez.500)).
   - His reading is that "Adam" is the spirit of Adam and "Eve" is His self. The "tree of good and evil" is the material world, and the serpent is "attachment to the material world" ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_432&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_f0.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_f0.445)) ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_433&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_f1.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_f1.469)).
   - In a pilgrim's account, He is reported to have called the creation of Adam and Eve an allegory ([Pilgrimage in March](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/ella-goodall_pilgrimage-in-march#p36)). He is also reported to have asked how anyone could accept Adam being born with no father or mother while doubting Christ's birth ([Pilgrimage to Haifa and 'Akka, November-December 1900](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/emogene-hoagg_pilgrimage-to-haifa-and-akka-november-december-1900#p284)).

3. *Physical origins.*
   - The Qur'án's stages of the embryo become a parallel for humanity as a whole. 'Abdu'l-Bahá says man's existence on this planet "must have traversed many stages" ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_646&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_kw.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_kw.896)) before reaching its present form, "like the embryo". Scholars disagree about how to read "species" here ([Origin of Complex Order in Biology: Abdu'l-Baha's concept of the origi…](https://bahai-library.com/kitzing_origin_complex_order&chapter=all)) ([Philosophical Conversations between 'Abdu'l-Bahá and Dr. Josephina Fal…](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/philosophical-conversations-between-abdul-baha-and-dr-josephina-fallscheer#p6)).

**The main difference:** the Torah and the Qur'án mainly give an account of origin. The Bahá'í texts mostly treat the Adam story as a symbol of the soul's relationship to the material world. They stress the nobility God placed in every person ("Noble I made thee" ([The Hidden Words of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/hidden-words-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_47&selectionString=the-hidden-words-prod_en_42.0~the-hidden-words-prod_en_42.360))) and the two lives of man. In 'Abdu'l-Bahá's words, "man has two lives, the material and the Spiritual" ([Pilgrimage to Haifa and 'Akka, November-December 1900](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/emogene-hoagg_pilgrimage-to-haifa-and-akka-november-december-1900#p199)).

I can go further into the symbolism of Adam and Eve in *Some Answered Questions*, or into the Bahá'í teaching on the soul, if you'd like.

messages.content: How do the Bahá’í writings and the Book of Mormon treat tithing?

perplexity.text:
The two traditions both treat giving as a religious obligation, but they define and administer it differently.

| Aspect | Bahá’í writings | Book of Mormon / Latter-day Saint practice |
|---|---|---|
| **Basic requirement** | The central financial law is **Ḥuqúqu’lláh** (“Right of God”), a fixed portion of accumulated wealth. Once a believer’s possessions reach the prescribed threshold, 19% is paid; thereafter, 19% of qualifying increases is due after necessary expenses. [9] | Tithing is **one-tenth of annual income or “interest.”** The later Latter-day Saint revelation describes it as “one-tenth of all their interest annually” and a standing law. [4][8] |
| **Basis of calculation** | Net wealth or increases in wealth, after expenses and debts—not simply gross income. [3][9] | Income/annual increase, conventionally understood by the Church as one-tenth of income. [4][8] |
| **How it is given** | It is a spiritual obligation left to individual conscience: believers are not to be individually pressured to pay it. Ḥuqúqu’lláh is distinct from voluntary contributions to Bahá’í funds. [5][9] | It is a commandment and a regular contribution to the Church. Tithing funds support Church buildings, congregations, programs, education, and other religious purposes. [8] |
| **Who administers it** | The Universal House of Justice receives and administers Ḥuqúqu’lláh; the law also envisions assistance for the poor and community needs. [3][5] | Church authorities administer tithes for the work of the Church; the Book of Mormon’s presentation connects tithing with bringing offerings into the Lord’s “storehouse.” [4][8] |
| **Spiritual meaning** | It is an act of obedience, purification, detachment from material possessions, and support for the common good. Payment should be made joyfully, when possible. [5][9] | It is an expression of faith, a test of priorities, and a commandment accompanied by promises of divine blessings, echoing the resurrected Christ’s teaching in 3 Nephi 24. [4][8] |

A key distinction is that the **Book of Mormon itself does not give the later “one-tenth of annual interest” formula in the same form as Doctrine and Covenants 119**. It preserves Christ’s teaching that the people should bring tithes into the storehouse in 3 Nephi 24, quoting Malachi; the specific Latter-day Saint administrative definition of tithing comes from later revelation. [4][7]

Thus, Bahá’í Ḥuqúqu’lláh is primarily a **19% levy on qualifying accumulated wealth or increases**, voluntarily discharged to the central Bahá’í institution, whereas Latter-day Saint tithing is a **10% recurring payment on income**, made to the Church as a standing commandment.

current.text:
**Short answer:** The Book of Mormon, in the library's copy, carries tithing only as Malachi's words. The Bahá'í Writings replace the old tithe with a different law, Ḥuqúqu'lláh ("the Right of God"), and also mention a tithe-like revenue for a future society.

**The Book of Mormon**
- The only tithing text I found in it is Malachi's passage. It reads: "Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say: Wherein have we robbed thee? ([Bible, 26-39 (Eze-Mal)](https://bahai-library.com/bible/bible-part6.html))
- I could not confirm any other tithing passage in the Book of Mormon, such as a stated rate. I have left those out.

**The Bahá'í Writings**
- **Ḥuqúqu'lláh is a different law, not a tithe.** Bahá'u'lláh ordains: "Should anyone acquire one hundred miṯhqáls of gold, nineteen miṯhqáls thereof are God's." ([Bahá’í Sacred Writings](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_532&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blhb.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blhb.1185))
- **It is levied on capital above a threshold.** It becomes payable once assessable possessions reach 19 miṯhqáls of gold, about 2.2 troy ounces. ([A Codification of the Law of Huqúqulláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/codification-of-the-law-of-huququllah_bahaullah/?paraId=para_23&selectionString=a_codification_of_the_law_of_huququllah_ocean_en-bl3l.0~a_codification_of_the_law_of_huququllah_ocean_en-bl3l.174)) It is generally payable once on a given amount, plus what that amount later earns. ([Additional Tablets and Extracts from Tablets Revealed by Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/additional-tablets-and-extracts-from-tablets-revealed-by-bahaullah/?paraId=para_51&selectionString=additional_tablets_and_extracts_bahai_ocean_en-bl3w.0~additional_tablets_and_extracts_bahai_ocean_en-bl3w.634))
- **Expenses come first.** 'Abdu'l-Bahá explained that a person first pays necessary expenses, and 19% of what is left is Ḥuqúq. ([Ḥuqúqu’lláh — The Right of God](https://oceanlibrary.com/huququllah-the-right-of-god_bahaullah/?paraId=para_176&selectionString=uququ_llah_the_right_of_god_ocean_en-bl6w.0~uququ_llah_the_right_of_god_ocean_en-bl6w.361))
- **The rate is not a tenth.** One scholarly bibliography loosely calls it a "voluntary tithe." ([The Babi and Baha'i Religions: An Annotated Bibliography](https://bahai-library.com/maceoin_annotated_bibliography&chapter=all)) The Writings themselves use "the Right of God."
- **Where it goes.** It is offered through the Universal House of Justice as Head of the Faith. It funds the promotion of the Faith and philanthropic purposes. ([The Kitáb-i-Aqdas](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah?paraId=fn_124))
- **It is spiritual and voluntary.** Paying it is a spiritual obligation left to each believer's conscience. ([The Kitáb-i-Aqdas](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah?paraId=fn_124)) Bahá'u'lláh forbids anyone to solicit it. It is to be offered "spontaneously and in a spirit of joy and fellowship." ([Additional Tablets and Extracts from Tablets Revealed by Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/additional-tablets-and-extracts-from-tablets-revealed-by-bahaullah/?paraId=para_90&selectionString=additional_tablets_and_extracts_bahai_ocean_en-bl4v.0~additional_tablets_and_extracts_bahai_ocean_en-bl4v.243))
- **Assemblies may not compel it.** Shoghi Effendi's secretary wrote that Assemblies must not oblige the friends to pay it. ([Messages to the Indian Subcontinent](https://oceanlibrary.com/messages-to-the-indian-subcontinent_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_3193&selectionString=messages_to_the_indian_subcontinent_en-bl28f.0~messages_to_the_indian_subcontinent_en-bl28f.417))
- **Appeals go to everyone, not to individuals.** The House of Justice says Ḥuqúqu'lláh and the other funds may not be demanded or solicited from individuals. ([huququllah-1-bahaullah-abdul-baha_en](https://oceanoflights.org/huququllah-1-bahaullah-abdul-baha-en/#:~:text=The%20House%20of%20Justice,friends%2C%20not%20to%20individuals))
- **It is kept apart from ordinary giving.** The House of Justice prefers that contributions to the Funds and Ḥuqúqu'lláh payments be kept as separate accounts. ([Lights of Guidance](https://oceanoflights.org/lights-of-guidance-baha-i-ocean-en/#:~:text=It%20would%20be%20preferable,%7Bid%3D%22para3905%22%20ilmid%3D%22bl2a1%22%20type%3D%22par%22%20language%3D%22en%22%7D))

**A tithe in the Bahá'í Writings proper**
- 'Abdu'l-Bahá describes a tithe as the first revenue of a future "storehouse." It is a graduated levy on surplus income, and no tithe is collected from someone whose income only covers necessary expenses. ([Lights of Guidance](https://oceanoflights.org/lights-of-guidance-baha-i-ocean-en/#:~:text=The%20first%20revenue%20is,%7Bid%3D%22para7022%22%20ilmid%3D%22bl4wm%22%20type%3D%22par%22%20language%3D%22en%22%7D))
- Tithes are the first of the storehouse's seven revenues. ([Additional Tablets, Extracts and Talks](https://oceanlibrary.com/additional-tablets-extracts-and-talks_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_181&selectionString=abdu_l_baha_additional_tablets_extracts_and_talks_430a4c77afa01f6eb5e4f2c4028e655d_82.0~abdu_l_baha_additional_tablets_extracts_and_talks_430a4c77afa01f6eb5e4f2c4028e655d_82.204))
- In one talk, reported in Star of the West, tithing is traced back to Abraham's gift to Melchizedek. The speaker presents the Bahá'í version as "originally the rights of God," now serving as "succour to the unfortunate." ([Star of the West](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/us-bahai-news_star-of-the-west#p922))

The Book of Mormon, as far as the library shows, repeats Malachi's call to bring tithes to the storehouse. The Bahá'í Writings keep the idea of a portion belonging to God. They change its rate, base, recipient and method, and they make payment a matter of conscience with no solicitation.

I can go further into Ḥuqúqu'lláh, for example how it is calculated, or into 'Abdu'l-Bahá's description of the storehouse.

messages.content: I’m trying to understand what Bahá’ís actually mean when they say Christ has returned.

perplexity.text:
When Bahá’ís say **“Christ has returned,” they do not mean that Jesus’s physical body or personal identity has reappeared**. They mean that the same divine authority, spiritual qualities, and role represented by Jesus have appeared again in a new Messenger of God—principally **Bahá’u’lláh**, with the Báb understood as the herald of his mission.[2][4]

The idea works like this:

- **One divine source, successive Messengers:** Bahá’ís regard Jesus, Moses, Muhammad, the Buddha, the Báb, and Bahá’u’lláh as distinct human individuals who nevertheless manifest the same divine Spirit and authority. Thus, “return” means the return of the spiritual reality, not the return of the same person.[1][2]
- **A biblical analogy:** Bahá’ís point to Jesus’ identification of John the Baptist with the promised return of Elijah. John was not literally Elijah resurrected; he came “in the spirit and power” of Elijah. Bahá’ís understand Bahá’u’lláh’s relationship to Christ similarly.[2][10]
- **Prophecy is fulfilled symbolically:** References to Christ coming “in the clouds,” with glory, or under a new name are interpreted spiritually rather than as predictions of a visible descent through the sky. “Clouds,” in this reading, can symbolize the obscuring effects of unfamiliarity, human expectations, and religious authority.[3]
- **The claim is already fulfilled:** Bahá’ís identify Bahá’u’lláh’s appearance in the nineteenth century as the promised return of Christ and the advent of God’s kingdom in a spiritual and social sense—not as the immediate physical transformation of the planet.[6]

So, in a single sentence: **Jesus has not returned as Jesus; Christ has “returned” because the divine Messenger who appeared in Bahá’u’lláh embodies the same Christ-like reality and continues the work of revealing God to humanity.**[1][2]

current.text:
Bahá'ís mean that the spirit and reality of Christ, the divine Word that spoke through Jesus, has appeared again in a new person, Bahá'u'lláh. They do not mean that Jesus of Nazareth has come back in his own body or personality.

**"Return" means the same reality in a new person**
- 'Abdu'l-Bahá says that when the Prophets spoke of a "return", they meant "not the return of the essence but of the attributes; it is not the return of the Manifestation Himself but of His perfections." ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_1005&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_uu.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_uu.533))
- His example is John the Baptist, who is called Elijah in the Gospel. That does not mean Elijah's "rational soul and personality" came back in John's body. It means Elijah's perfections and attributes became manifest in John. ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_1005&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_uu.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_uu.533))
- He also uses the image of a lamp: when another lamp is lit tonight, "we say that the light of last night is shining again." ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_1006&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_uv.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_uv.961)) The same applies to spring flowers, which are said to "return" each year. ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_1006&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_uv.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_uv.961))
- So Bahá'u'lláh is the return of Christ in the way John was the return of Elijah. Jesus' spiritual reality, with its light and authority, shines again in a new lamp.

**The "clouds of heaven" are read symbolically**
- Bahá'u'lláh interprets the prophecy of the Son of Man coming "in the clouds of heaven" ([Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_735&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_n5.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_n5.973)) in the Kitáb-i-Íqán. ([The Kitáb-i-Íqán](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah/?paraId=para_89&selectionString=kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_58.0~kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_58.932))
- 'Abdu'l-Bahá refers readers to that interpretation for the signs of Christ's return. ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_381&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_dl.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_dl.572))
- Bahá'u'lláh also addresses Christians directly. He quotes Jesus' words "I go away, and come again unto you" and asks why they did not draw near when He "did come again unto you in the clouds of heaven." ([Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_735&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_n5.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_n5.973))
- In another passage He says Jesus "hath once more, in My person, been made manifest." ([A Hymn to Love (Sáqí, bi-dih ábí)](https://bahai-library.com/savi_hymn_love))

**Christ's return is also the Father's glory**
- A letter on behalf of Shoghi Effendi says Bahá'u'lláh's advent "marks the return of the Son in the glory of the Father." ([Resurrection and Return of Jesus](https://bahai-library.com/uhj_resurrection_return_jesus))
- The same letter says that the Son's appearance after the calamitous events means "the revelation of His full glory and its recognition and acceptance by the peoples of the world, and not His physical appearance." ([Resurrection and Return of Jesus](https://bahai-library.com/uhj_resurrection_return_jesus))
- Another letter on behalf of Shoghi Effendi links Christ's prophecy of His return, the coming of the Kingdom of the Father, with the worldwide realization of Bahá'u'lláh's sovereignty. ([Resurrection and Return of Jesus](https://bahai-library.com/uhj_resurrection_return_jesus)) Shoghi Effendi himself calls Bahá'u'lláh "the Establisher of the Kingdom of the Father foretold by the Son." ([The Promised Day is Come](https://oceanlibrary.com/promised-day-is-come_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_340&selectionString=the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-blbk.0~the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-blbk.1120))
- For Bahá'ís, then, the return is both a fact, since Bahá'u'lláh has already appeared, and a process, as His station is recognized across the world.

**This does not diminish Jesus**
In this view Christ is one continuing divine reality that appears "in each of the cycles" ([Bahá’u’lláh and the New Era](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahaullah-and-the-new-era_john-esslemont/?paraId=para_1252&selectionString=baha_u_llah_and_the_new_era_bahai_ocean_en-blzb.0~baha_u_llah_and_the_new_era_bahai_ocean_en-blzb.659)), and Jesus is one of its appearances. The words are attributed to Bahá'u'lláh in a text of the library, and they say Christ "came with His Kingdom from the beginning which hath no beginning, and will come with His Kingdom to the eternity of eternities." ([Bahá’u’lláh and the New Era](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahaullah-and-the-new-era_john-esslemont/?paraId=para_1252&selectionString=baha_u_llah_and_the_new_era_bahai_ocean_en-blzb.0~baha_u_llah_and_the_new_era_bahai_ocean_en-blzb.659)) The return of Christ is therefore not a rival to Jesus. It is the same Word, spoken again in a new person.

I can go further into how Bahá'ís read the specific signs, such as the darkened sun and falling stars, or how they read "the Spirit of Truth".

args.query: Bahá'u'lláh: the Spirit of Truth, the Promised One of all ages, Christ has come again in the glory of the Father
'Abdu'l-Bahá Some Answered Questions return of Christ, the same reality, Elijah and John the Baptist
Shoghi Effendi Bahá'u'lláh the return of Christ in the glory of the Father
Kitáb-i-Íqán Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven, return of Christ interpreted

current.why: Builds the answer on the right authorities, in their own words: 'Abdu'l-Bahá on return as the return of attributes rather than essence, the Elijah/John example and the lamp image (Some Answered Questions); Bahá'u'lláh in Gleanings and the Íqán; letters on behalf of Shoghi Effendi on 'the return of the Son in the glory of the Father'; and The Promised Day is Come. It offers a clear way to go further. Weak points: one quotation comes through Esslemont, though the answer hedges it, and the 'Hymn to Love' source for the 'in My person' line is uncertain. Some letters are cited through a compilation with a House-labelled URL, but the authority quoted is the Guardian's.

perplexity.why: The summary is accurate: spiritual reality rather than the person, Elijah/John 'in the spirit and power', and the clouds read symbolically. But it quotes none of the Writings and names no authoritative source; its numbered citations are opaque. It reads like a generic encyclopedia entry, with none of the textual substance a reader of the Writings is looking for.

verdict.gaps: B was more concise and gave Luke's 'spirit and power of Elijah' phrase, plus a short note on what the clouds symbolise (human expectations, religious authority), which A left implicit. Otherwise none.

messages.content: Help me understand the Bahá’í teaching on infallibility — I find it confusing.

perplexity.text:
The Bahá’í teaching becomes clearer if **“infallibility” is divided into different meanings**. It does not mean that every Bahá’í, or every statement made by a religious leader, is automatically correct.

## 1. Essential infallibility

Bahá’u’lláh and the other universal **Manifestations of God**—such as Abraham, Moses, Buddha, Christ, Muhammad, and the Báb—are described as possessing *essential infallibility*. This means that their revelation of God’s will is not merely a fallible personal opinion: their teachings and authoritative commands are understood to express divine truth for their age.[2]

“Essential” means inseparable from their station. They are not simply unusually wise people who happen never to make mistakes; they occupy a unique role as the channels through which God’s guidance is revealed.[2]

## 2. Conferred infallibility

Other figures or institutions may possess **conferred infallibility**. This is not intrinsic to their personal nature. Rather, God is understood to protect them from error **within a specific religious function**.[1][2]

In the Bahá’í writings, this category applies in different ways to:

- **‘Abdu’l-Bahá**, the son of Bahá’u’lláh and authorized interpreter of His teachings.
- **Shoghi Effendi**, the Guardian of the Bahá’í Faith and authorized interpreter after ‘Abdu’l-Bahá.
- **The Universal House of Justice**, particularly as a functioning institution rather than as individually infallible people.[1][3]

## 3. The Universal House of Justice

The distinction between the **individual members** and the **institution** is crucial. Individual members are not regarded as essentially infallible; the protection is associated with the House of Justice acting as a body.[1]

Its infallibility concerns its divinely assigned sphere: deciding questions not explicitly settled in the Bahá’í scriptures and applying the teachings to changing conditions. It does **not** mean that the institution is omniscient, knows every scientific fact, or cannot revise a decision when relevant facts change.[1][10]

## 4. Infallibility is not omniscience

A person or institution can be protected from making an error in a particular authoritative religious decision without possessing unlimited knowledge. Shoghi Effendi, for example, is described as not being an infallible authority on economics, science, or technical subjects; his authority concerned interpretation and application of the Bahá’í teachings.[10]

So the claim is not:

> “This person knows everything.”

It is closer to:

> “In this defined role, God protects the authoritative guidance given through this person or institution from religious error.”

## 5. What about ordinary believers?

Ordinary Bahá’ís—including scholars, administrators, and local or national assemblies—are **not infallible**. Individual interpretation is encouraged, but it remains personal and may be mistaken. The Bahá’í writings therefore emphasize humility, prayer, study, willingness to revise one’s views, and deference to the authoritative texts and institutions.[3]

## A simple analogy

Think of three levels:

| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Manifestation of God** | Essential infallibility: the source of divine revelation for an age |
| **Authorized interpreter** | Conferred authority and protection in interpreting the revelation |
| **Universal House of Justice** | Conferred protection when acting collectively within its prescribed institutional sphere |
| **Individual believer** | No infallibility; sincere understanding can still be mistaken |

The shortest summary is: **Bahá’í infallibility is authority-specific, not a claim that every religious figure is omniscient or personally incapable of error.** The central distinction is between the Manifestation’s essential infallibility and the limited, conferred infallibility associated with designated interpreters and the Universal House of Justice.[1][2]

current.text:
Bahá'í teaching describes two kinds of infallibility. One belongs to the Manifestations of God by nature. The other is a protection from error that God gives to certain people and institutions.

**1. Essential infallibility: the Manifestations of God**

'Abdu'l-Bahá says that "infallibility in essence is confined to the universal Manifestations of God; for infallibility is an essential requirement of Their reality, and the essential requirement of a thing is inseparable from the thing itself." ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_612&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_jz.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_jz.868)) His image is that rays cannot be separated from the sun, and if they could, "it would not be the sun." ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_612&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_jz.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_jz.868)) So whatever the Manifestation says is "the utterance of God." ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_615&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_k2.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_k2.809))

A letter written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi ties this to the idea of revelation itself. "The whole theory of Divine Revelation rests on the infallibility of the Prophet… If They are not infallible, then They are not divine." ([Messages from the Universal House of Justice: 1986-2001](https://bahai-library.com/3819)) Bahá'u'lláh calls this the "Most Great Infallibility," and says it is "restricted to the Manifestations of Command." ([Responses to Questions of Manakji Sahib](http://whoisBahá’u’lláh.com/windflower/translations-on-this-site/translations/140-responses-to-questions-of-manakji-sahib))

**2. Conferred infallibility: protected souls and institutions**

'Abdu'l-Bahá calls this infallibility "as an attribute." It is "not an essential requirement; rather, it is a ray of the gift of infallibility which shines from the Sun of Truth upon certain hearts." These souls "are not essentially infallible, yet they are under the care, protection, and unerring guidance of God." ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_613&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_k0.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_k0.769)) He gives the reason: they are channels of grace, and if they erred they would lead the faithful into error. ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_613&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_k0.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_k0.769)) The comparison he uses elsewhere is that the sun's light is intrinsic, while a planet's light is borrowed from the sun. ([Pilgrimage to Haifa and 'Akká with Tablets translations](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/ali-kuli-khan_pilgrimage-to-haifa-and-akka-with-tablets-translations#p99))

Two institutions are named as holders of this conferred infallibility:

- **The Universal House of Justice.** If it is properly elected, its decisions on matters "not explicitly recorded in the Book" ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_614&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_k1.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_k1.668)) will be "guarded from error." The individual members "are not essentially infallible," but "the body" is under God's guidance. ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_614&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_k1.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_k1.668)) The Will and Testament says the Guardian and the House are "under the care and protection of the Abhá Beauty, under the shelter and unerring guidance of His Holiness the Exalted One. Whatsoever they decide is of God." ([Bahá’í Sacred Writings](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_1823&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bl1hi.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bl1hi.1958))
- **The Guardian.** His infallibility is limited in scope (see below).

**Where the confusion usually arises: scope**

Conferred infallibility is not omniscience, and it does not make a person infallible in everything.

- Shoghi Effendi's infallibility "is confined to matters which are related strictly to the Cause and interpretation of the teachings." He was "not an infallible authority on other subjects, such as economics, science." ([Uncompiled Published Letters](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_8609&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl88x.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl88x.439))
- The House of Justice summarises his replies. He was "not, like the Prophet, omniscient at will." ([Lights of Guidance: A Bahá’í Reference File](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/compilations/helen-hornby_lights-of-guidance-a-bahai-reference-file#p3693)) His infallibility covers interpretation and its application, and also protection of the Faith. ([Lights of Guidance: A Bahá’í Reference File](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/compilations/helen-hornby_lights-of-guidance-a-bahai-reference-file#p3693))
- The House of Justice's own infallibility operates "within its ordained sphere." It does not depend on a Guardian being a member. ([Lights of Guidance](https://oceanoflights.org/lights-of-guidance-baha-i-ocean-en/#:~:text=The%20infallibility%20of%20the,%7Bid%3D%22para4011%22%20ilmid%3D%22bl2cw%22%20type%3D%22par%22%20language%3D%22en%22%7D))
- Interpretation and legislation are separate spheres. Shoghi Effendi wrote that neither the Guardian nor the House "can, nor will ever, infringe upon the sacred and prescribed domain of the other." ([Lights of Guidance](https://oceanoflights.org/lights-of-guidance-baha-i-ocean-en/#:~:text=The%20infallibility%20of%20the,%7Bid%3D%22para4011%22%20ilmid%3D%22bl2cw%22%20type%3D%22par%22%20language%3D%22en%22%7D))

**A point that is easy to miss**

The two kinds of infallibility differ in kind, not only in degree. Essential infallibility comes from the Manifestation's own reality. Conferred infallibility depends entirely on a relationship, like the moon reflecting the sun. One writer says Shoghi Effendi saw himself as a satellite and "would have been horrified" to be called "a second Moon." ([Shoghi Effendi: The Range and Power of His Pen](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/ali-nakhjavani_shoghi-effendi-the-range-and-power-of-his-pen#p26)) This is also why Bahá'ís can hold both that the House's rulings are protected and that its members are ordinary individuals.

I can go on to how the House of Justice applies this to its own rulings, or to the Tablet of Bahá'u'lláh on the "Most Great Infallibility," if either would help.

messages.content: Why would God send more than one Messenger? I want to get the reasoning, not a list of names.

perplexity.text:
The basic reasoning is that **one divine message may need to be repeatedly delivered, locally communicated, practically embodied, and restored after people distort or neglect it**.

From an Islamic perspective:

- **Humanity is spread across different peoples and languages.** A messenger addressing one community would not automatically make the message equally accessible to every other community. The Qur’an presents messengers as speaking clearly in the language of their own people.[1]
- **People do not remain unchanged.** Over generations, teachings can be forgotten, altered, mixed with superstition, or used to serve power. A later messenger can restore the original call rather than introduce a different God or purpose.[2][4]
- **Different eras may require different laws or applications.** The central message—worship God and live rightly—can remain constant while detailed rules address a community’s particular circumstances.[2][5]
- **A messenger is not merely a delivery mechanism.** People need a visible human example of how revelation is practiced under real pressures. Multiple messengers allow guidance to be embodied in different societies and conditions.[2]
- **Multiple messengers reinforce moral responsibility.** Repeated warnings remove the excuse that people were left without guidance, while also giving communities renewed opportunities to return to truth.[2][7]
- **Several messengers can cooperate.** One may support another, share the burden, or clarify the same mission for a larger or more resistant population.[1]

So the point is not that God needed several attempts to communicate one idea. Rather, **the recipients were different, history changed, communities drifted, and guidance had to remain accessible and compelling in real human circumstances**. In this view, the plurality of messengers reflects the continuity of one source and one fundamental call, expressed through successive acts of guidance—not competing religions.[1][4]

current.text:
God sends more than one Messenger because the Messengers are one reality and humanity is not static. Two reasons in the Writings explain this: humanity's capacity changes, and so do its needs.

**1. The Messengers are not rivals. They are one light from different horizons.**
'Abdu'l-Bahá says "All the Divine Manifestations are one reality, but they have appeared from various dawning points," as the sun rises from different points on the horizon ([Abdu'l-Bahá at Theosophical Society, San Francisco Lodge, on 11 Octobe…](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/core-talks/abdul-baha-recorded_abdul-baha-at-theosophical-society-san-francisco-lodge-on-11-october-1912#p27)). So the question is not why God sends several different messengers. It is why the same Sun rises again. Bahá'u'lláh says that "all the days are but one and the same" is true, and so is the claim that they differ in name and character ([Loom of Reality](https://bahai-library.com/inventory/subjects/95CF4C3DD18F4844902B686B6DF805D2)). The apparent differences in what they say come from "this difference in their station and mission," not from any contradiction in the Truth itself ([The Kitáb-i-Íqán](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah/?paraId=para_204&selectionString=kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_8g.0~kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_8g.467)).

**2. Revelation is given in proportion to what people can bear.**
Bahá'u'lláh writes that "in every Dispensation the light of Divine Revelation hath been vouchsafed unto men in direct proportion to their spiritual capacity." ([Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_240&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_9f.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_9f.873)) He compares this to the sun, whose rays are feeble at first and grow stronger as it rises. If it released all its energy at once, it "would, no doubt, cause injury to all created things" ([Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_240&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_9f.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_9f.873)). The Word works the same way. Shoghi Effendi quotes Bahá'u'lláh: "Should the Word be allowed to release suddenly all the energies latent within it, no man could sustain the weight of so mighty a Revelation" ([The Promised Day is Come](https://oceanlibrary.com/promised-day-is-come_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_327&selectionString=the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-blba.0~the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-blba.1646)). A single, final revelation would be too much for humanity early on and too little later.

**3. The needs of each age differ, so the remedy differs.**
Bahá'u'lláh says: "The All-Knowing Physician hath His finger on the pulse of mankind… Every age hath its own problem… The remedy the world needeth in its present-day afflictions can never be the same as that which a subsequent age may require" ([Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_647&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_kp.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_kp.396)). A physician who changes the prescription as the patient's condition changes is not contradicting himself. It would be wrong to keep the old prescription once the physician has ordered a new one ([Bahá’u’lláh and the New Era](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahaullah-and-the-new-era_john-esslemont/?paraId=para_726&selectionString=baha_u_llah_and_the_new_era_bahai_ocean_en-blka.0~baha_u_llah_and_the_new_era_bahai_ocean_en-blka.840)).

**4. Humanity is being educated.**
'Abdu'l-Bahá compares the Manifestations to teachers in a school. They taught "the children of mankind from age to age in those lessons for which they were adapted," so that humanity might advance through the classes to "the highest classes of perfection" ([Star of the West](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/us-bahai-news_star-of-the-west-2#p375)). He also says of Christ's coming: the teachings had "the same basic principles" as Bahá'u'lláh's, but were given "in accordance with the infancy of the human race," whereas Bahá'u'lláh's are suited to "the stage of the maturity of the world" ([Star of the West](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/us-bahai-news_star-of-the-west-7#p743)).

**What stays the same and what changes.**
'Abdu'l-Bahá puts it this way: "The foundation of all the religions is one and this foundation is truth." The subsidiary laws "that pertain to the affairs of society differ," because they "are subject to the demands of time and place" ([Mahmud's Diary: The Diary of Mirza Mahmud-i-Zarqani Chronicling 'Abdu'…](https://bahai-library.com/zarqani_mahmuds_diary&chapter=all)). The next Messenger does not cancel the last one. He renews the same springtime, so "each springtime is identical with the former springtime" and differs only in the calendar ([The Promulgation of Universal Peace](https://oceanlibrary.com/promulgation-of-universal-peace_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_1220&selectionString=promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_10n.0~promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_10n.1717)).

**Shoghi Effendi's summary.**
He gives the principle as "Religious truth is not absolute but relative," ([Statement to the Special U.N. Committee on Palestine, 1947](https://oceanlibrary.com/summary-statement_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_11&selectionString=special_un_committee_on_palestine_1947_bahai_ocean11ae336bb52626b3cf292e0e8c2e4461-bl35.0~special_un_committee_on_palestine_1947_bahai_ocean11ae336bb52626b3cf292e0e8c2e4461-bl35.539)) and says revelation is "a continuous and progressive process." The great religions are "complementary" and their missions "represent successive stages in the spiritual evolution of human society" ([Statement to the Special U.N. Committee on Palestine, 1947](https://oceanlibrary.com/summary-statement_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_11&selectionString=special_un_committee_on_palestine_1947_bahai_ocean11ae336bb52626b3cf292e0e8c2e4461-bl35.0~special_un_committee_on_palestine_1947_bahai_ocean11ae336bb52626b3cf292e0e8c2e4461-bl35.539)). For the same reason he says the Bahá'í Revelation "emphatically repudiates the claim to be regarded as the final revelation of God's will" ([The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_292&selectionString=shoghi_effendi_world_order_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_en_al.0~shoghi_effendi_world_order_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_en_al.1210)).

I can go further into why each Messenger has two stations, one of essential unity and one of distinct mission, if you'd like.

Shoghi Effendi religious truth is not absolute but relative, Divine revelation is progressive, not final
'Abdu'l-Bahá Some Answered Questions spring season Christ Muhammad the Sun of Truth the divine religions foundation is one, they differ in non-essentials
